guides.title: How to Prepare for IC-38 Exam in 7 Days: Study Plan
guides.description: A practical 7-day IC-38 study plan with chapter-wise daily targets, revision slots and timed mock tests to help you prepare well for the IRDAI agent exam.
guides.primary: how to prepare for ic 38 exam
guides.intro: If you are wondering how to prepare for IC 38 exam without losing weeks to it, the answer is a short, structured plan. IC-38 is the IRDAI pre-recruitment exam for insurance agents and point-of-sale persons, and its syllabus is concept-heavy rather than calculation-heavy. Most candidates who already have the study material from their insurer or training institute can cover it properly in seven focused days of two to three hours each. This guide gives you a day-by-day plan, tells you which chapters tend to carry more questions, and shows where mock tests and revision fit so that you walk into the exam calm and ready.

sections.heading: IC-38 exam pattern at a glance
paragraphs: Our mock tests follow an indicative pattern of 50 multiple-choice questions, 50 marks and 60 minutes, with no negative marking. Treat this as indicative — confirm in the latest official notification, because the Insurance Institute of India and IRDAI can revise the number of questions, the pass percentage and the format for life, general, health or composite licences. Check insuranceinstituteofindia.com and your insurer's licensing team for current details.

With roughly a minute or more per question and no penalty for wrong answers, IC-38 is not a speed test. It rewards clear understanding of insurance principles, product features and regulations. That is why a short plan works: you are learning a fixed body of concepts, not building years of aptitude.
bullets: Questions: 50 (indicative)
Duration: 60 minutes (indicative)
Negative marking: none in the indicative pattern — attempt every question
Mode: computer-based, usually at an authorised centre or online as per current rules

sections.heading: Chapter weightage: where to spend your time
paragraphs: Based on the syllabus, the chapters you will study are Introduction to Insurance, Customer Service and Grievances, Regulatory Aspects of Agency, Legal Principles of Insurance, Life Insurance and Financial Planning, Life Insurance Products, Pricing and Valuation, Documentation and Underwriting, Life Insurance Claims, Health Insurance and General Insurance. Exact weightage is not published as a fixed table, so treat the guidance below as approximate.

Documentation and Underwriting, Health Insurance, Life Insurance Products, Legal Principles and General Insurance tend to produce a larger share of questions because they contain many definitions and rules. Pricing and Valuation, Claims and Financial Planning are smaller but easy to score once you learn the terms.
bullets: Higher share (approximately): Documentation & Underwriting, Health Insurance, Life Insurance Products, Legal Principles, General Insurance
Medium share: Introduction to Insurance, Customer Service & Grievances, Regulatory Aspects of Agency
Smaller share: Life Insurance & Financial Planning, Pricing & Valuation, Life Insurance Claims

sections.heading: The 7-day IC-38 study plan
paragraphs: Plan for two to three hours on weekdays and a little more on the last two days. Read each chapter once with attention, write short notes of definitions and numbers such as free-look periods or grace periods as given in your study material, and solve chapter questions the same day. Always check numbers against the current official material, since regulations change.
bullets: Day 1: Introduction to Insurance and Legal Principles (utmost good faith, insurable interest, indemnity, subrogation, contribution, proximate cause) — 30 chapter questions
Day 2: Regulatory Aspects of Agency and Customer Service & Grievances (agent code of conduct, licensing, ombudsman, grievance redressal) — 30 questions
Day 3: Life Insurance & Financial Planning and Life Insurance Products (term, endowment, whole life, ULIPs, riders) — 40 questions
Day 4: Pricing & Valuation, Documentation & Underwriting (proposal form, KYC, medical and non-medical underwriting) — 40 questions
Day 5: Life Insurance Claims, Health Insurance and General Insurance (claim types, cashless and reimbursement, motor, fire, property basics) — 40 questions
Day 6: First full-length timed mock test in the morning, detailed review in the evening, re-read your two weakest chapters
Day 7: Second full-length mock test, quick revision of your notes and definitions, light reading only in the last two hours

sections.heading: How to study each chapter efficiently
paragraphs: IC-38 questions are mostly direct: a definition, a feature of a product, the right step in a process, or the correct principle for a situation. Read actively. After each topic, close the book and explain the concept in one or two sentences. If you cannot, read it again.

Create a one-page sheet for terms that look alike, such as indemnity versus subrogation, surrender value versus paid-up value, or a rider versus a base policy. Many wrong answers in this exam come from confusing two similar terms rather than not knowing either.
bullets: Highlight every term in bold in your study material and write a one-line meaning
Group regulatory points (agent duties, prohibited practices) into a single list
Practise situation questions: 'Which principle applies when...' style items
Revise your sheet for ten minutes before starting each new day

sections.heading: Revision and mock-test schedule
paragraphs: Mock tests are where the plan comes together. Taking full-length timed mock tests on Days 6 and 7, and reviewing the explanation for every question you got wrong or guessed, is the fastest way to find gaps. Do not just look at your score; note the chapter of each mistake and go back to that page of your notes.

If your scores are steady and your mistakes are scattered rather than concentrated in one chapter, you are close to ready. If one chapter keeps causing errors, spend an extra hour on it before the exam. Our practice questions are original and written to the syllabus — they are for practice, not a copy of what you will see.
bullets: After each chapter: 20–40 practice questions
Day 6: Mock test 1 + 90-minute error review
Day 7: Mock test 2 + 60-minute review + final notes revision
Exam morning: one short read of your one-page sheet, nothing new

sections.heading: Exam-day tips for IC-38
paragraphs: Reach the centre early with the documents your insurer or the exam body asks for, and confirm the reporting time and ID requirements in your hall ticket or official communication. Inside, read each question fully; words like 'not', 'except' and 'first' change the answer.

Since there is no negative marking in the indicative pattern, never leave a question blank. Mark doubtful ones, finish the paper, then return to them with the time you have left. Most candidates finish with ten to twenty minutes to spare, so use that time to recheck questions on principles and regulations.

sections.heading: Common mistakes to avoid
paragraphs: The biggest mistake is reading the material once and skipping practice. The second is memorising numbers from an old guide instead of the current syllabus. A third is ignoring the smaller chapters; Claims and Pricing are short, and leaving them out throws away easy marks.
bullets: Studying from outdated notes — always use the current official study material
Skipping Health and General Insurance if you are taking a life licence, without checking whether they are in your syllabus
Not reviewing mock-test mistakes
Cramming new chapters on the last day

faqs: Is 7 days enough to prepare for the IC-38 exam?

For most candidates, yes. The syllabus is conceptual, and two to three focused hours a day for a week is usually enough to read every chapter, practise questions and take two full mock tests. If you are new to insurance terms or can study only an hour a day, stretch the plan to 10–14 days.
Is there negative marking in the IC-38 exam?

In the indicative pattern used for our mock tests there is no negative marking, so you should attempt every question. Rules can change, so confirm the current marking scheme in the latest official communication from the Insurance Institute of India or your insurer before your exam date.
Which chapters are most important for IC-38?

Based on the syllabus, Documentation and Underwriting, Health Insurance, Life Insurance Products, Legal Principles and General Insurance tend to carry more questions. Do not skip smaller chapters such as Claims and Pricing, though; they are short and easy to score once the key terms are clear.

guides.title: IC-38 Syllabus Explained Chapter by Chapter
guides.description: IC-38 syllabus explained in plain English: what each chapter covers, the key terms to learn and the type of questions to expect in the IRDAI agent exam.
guides.intro: The IC 38 syllabus looks long on paper, but it is really a tour of how insurance works: the principles behind it, the products agents sell, the paperwork, claims and the rules agents must follow. Knowing what each chapter is actually about helps you study with purpose instead of reading pages blindly. This guide walks through the syllabus chapter by chapter, lists the terms most worth learning, and explains the type of question each chapter tends to produce. Use it alongside your official study material, which remains the final word on scope, and confirm the latest syllabus with the Insurance Institute of India.

sections.heading: How the IC-38 syllabus is organised
paragraphs: IC-38 is the pre-recruitment exam for insurance agents and point-of-sale persons. The Insurance Institute of India prepares the study material, and the syllabus differs slightly for life, general, health and composite licences. Our indicative mock-test pattern is 50 questions in 60 minutes with no negative marking — indicative, confirm in the latest official notification at insuranceinstituteofindia.com.

The chapters fall into four blocks: foundations (introduction and legal principles), products (life, health and general), process (documentation, underwriting, pricing and claims) and conduct (regulation and customer service). Studying block by block makes it easier to see how ideas connect.

sections.heading: Foundations: Introduction to Insurance and Legal Principles
paragraphs: Introduction to Insurance explains risk, the pooling of premiums from many people to pay the losses of a few, the history of insurance in India and the role of insurance in the economy. Questions are usually definitional: what insurance does, what risk management means, and which risks are insurable.

Legal Principles of Insurance is one of the most important chapters. It covers the elements of a valid contract and the core principles of insurance. Expect situation questions that ask which principle applies.

A useful way to remember the legal principles is to attach each one to a simple everyday example. Insurable interest: you can insure your own house but not a stranger's. Utmost good faith: you must disclose a known heart condition in a life proposal. Proximate cause: a fire that follows a storm may be treated differently from a storm that damages a roof directly. Examples like these make situation questions much easier.
bullets: Utmost good faith (uberrimae fidei) and material facts
Insurable interest — who can insure what
Indemnity, subrogation and contribution (mainly general insurance)
Proximate cause — the dominant cause of a loss
Offer, acceptance, consideration and capacity to contract

sections.heading: Products: Life, Health and General Insurance
paragraphs: Life Insurance and Financial Planning introduces the human life value concept, life stages and why people need protection and savings. Life Insurance Products then covers term plans, endowment, whole life, money-back, unit-linked plans and riders. Learn what each product is designed for and its key features; comparison questions are common.

Health Insurance covers hospitalisation policies, family floater plans, critical illness, top-up cover, cashless and reimbursement claims, and the role of third-party administrators. General Insurance introduces motor, fire, property, marine and liability covers at a basic level. Check whether your licence type includes all of these chapters.

When comparing products, focus on three questions for each one: who is it meant for, does it have a savings or investment element, and what happens at maturity or on death. Writing a small comparison table with these three columns for term, endowment, whole life, money-back and unit-linked plans covers a large share of product questions in a single page of notes.
bullets: Term vs endowment vs ULIP: purpose, savings element, risk
Riders: what they add and when they apply
Health: sum insured, waiting periods, co-payment, exclusions — learn terms from current material
Motor: own damage vs third-party liability

sections.heading: Process: Documentation, Underwriting, Pricing and Claims
paragraphs: Documentation and Underwriting is usually the heaviest chapter. It covers the proposal form, KYC, age proof, medical and non-medical underwriting, and how an insurer decides whether to accept a risk and on what terms. Learn the purpose of each document and the sequence from proposal to policy issue.

Pricing and Valuation explains, at a basic level, how premiums are set (mortality, interest, expenses), bonuses and surplus. Life Insurance Claims covers maturity, survival benefit and death claims, nomination, assignment and the documents required. These chapters are shorter, so a single careful reading plus practice questions usually suffices.
bullets: Proposal form, free-look period and policy document — verify current rules
Standard, sub-standard and declined lives
Nomination vs assignment
Early vs non-early death claims

sections.heading: Conduct: Regulatory Aspects and Customer Service
paragraphs: Regulatory Aspects of Agency covers who regulates insurance, how agents are licensed, the code of conduct, commission rules at a broad level and practices agents must avoid, such as mis-selling or rebating. These questions are often straightforward if you have read the rules once.

Customer Service and Grievances explains why service matters, how grievances are handled, the role of the insurance ombudsman and the protections for policyholders. Expect questions on the correct escalation path and the agent's role in after-sales service.

sections.heading: Approximate chapter weightage
paragraphs: There is no officially published fixed weightage, but based on the syllabus and the depth of each chapter, the split below is a reasonable guide for planning. Use it to decide how long to spend, not to skip anything.
bullets: Higher: Documentation & Underwriting, Health Insurance, Life Insurance Products, Legal Principles, General Insurance
Medium: Introduction to Insurance, Regulatory Aspects of Agency, Customer Service & Grievances
Lower: Life Insurance & Financial Planning, Pricing & Valuation, Life Insurance Claims

sections.heading: Terms that candidates most often confuse
paragraphs: Across the syllabus, a handful of pairs and groups of terms account for a large share of wrong answers. Learning them side by side, with one example each, is one of the quickest ways to raise your accuracy. Write each pair on a single line in your notes and test yourself until you can explain the difference in one sentence.

Situation questions are the other common trap. A question may describe a policyholder, a loss and a claim, and ask which principle or rule applies. Practise reading the scenario, underlining the key fact and matching it to the principle before you look at the options.
bullets: Indemnity vs subrogation vs contribution
Nomination vs assignment
Surrender value vs paid-up value
Cashless vs reimbursement claim
Medical vs non-medical underwriting
Grievance with the insurer vs complaint to the insurance ombudsman

sections.heading: How to use this syllabus while preparing
paragraphs: Turn each chapter into a checklist of the terms above and tick them off only when you can explain them without notes. Practise chapter-wise questions as soon as you finish reading, then take full-length timed mock tests once all chapters are covered and review the explanation for every mistake.

Keep your official study material as the base text. Guides like this one simplify and organise; they cannot replace the current syllabus, which may be updated by the Insurance Institute of India or IRDAI. Before your exam, check insuranceinstituteofindia.com and irdai.gov.in for any revision.

faqs: How many chapters are in the IC-38 syllabus?

The study material is organised into chapters covering insurance basics, legal principles, life, health and general insurance products, documentation and underwriting, pricing, claims, regulation and customer service. The exact number and order depend on the licence type and edition, so check the current material from the Insurance Institute of India.
Is the IC-38 syllabus the same for life and general insurance agents?

The foundation chapters overlap, but the product, underwriting and claims chapters differ between life, general, health and composite licences. Confirm which modules apply to your licence with your insurer's licensing team and the official syllabus before you start studying.
Which IC-38 chapter is the hardest?

Most candidates find Documentation and Underwriting and Legal Principles the hardest, because they contain many similar-sounding terms and situation-based questions. Make a one-page sheet of definitions for these chapters and practise applying each principle to short scenarios.

guides.title: How to Prepare for IBPS PO Prelims in 60 Days
guides.description: A realistic 60-day IBPS PO prelims study plan with week-by-week targets for Quant, Reasoning and English, plus a revision and mock test schedule that works.
guides.primary: how to prepare for ibps po prelims
guides.intro: Sixty days is a realistic window if you want to know how to prepare for IBPS PO prelims seriously while working or studying. The prelims tests three sections — English Language, Quantitative Aptitude and Reasoning Ability — under tight time pressure, so preparation is as much about speed and selection as it is about concepts. This guide lays out an eight-week plan with weekly targets, explains approximately how marks are spread across topics, and shows when to start full mocks and how to analyse them. It assumes three to four hours a day; adjust the pace if you have more or less time.

sections.heading: IBPS PO prelims pattern (indicative)
paragraphs: Our mock tests follow an indicative pattern of 100 questions, 100 marks and 60 minutes, with 0.25 of a mark deducted for each wrong answer. In recent cycles the paper has been split into three sections with separate time limits. Treat all of this as indicative — confirm in the latest official notification on ibps.in, which also lists eligibility, dates and the number of sections.

Because the overall cut-off and sectional cut-offs both matter, you cannot afford a weak section. The plan below gives each section steady time every week rather than finishing one subject before starting the next.
bullets: English Language: roughly 30 questions (approximately)
Quantitative Aptitude: roughly 35 questions (approximately)
Reasoning Ability: roughly 35 questions (approximately)
Negative marking: 0.25 per wrong answer (indicative)

sections.heading: Topic weightage: what to master first
paragraphs: Based on the syllabus and the usual shape of the paper, a few topics carry most of the marks. In Quant, Data Interpretation and simplification or approximation give the most questions, followed by number series, quadratic equations and arithmetic. In Reasoning, puzzles and seating arrangements dominate, with inequalities, syllogism, coding-decoding, blood relations and direction sense making up the rest. In English, reading comprehension, cloze test, error spotting and para jumbles are the core.
Start with the high-weight topics and keep the smaller ones for weeks four to six. That way, even if time runs short, the topics that decide your score are already strong.

sections.heading: The 60-day week-by-week plan
paragraphs: Each day, split your time across all three sections: about 75 minutes Quant, 75 minutes Reasoning, 45 minutes English and 15 minutes of revision notes. Read one editorial or long article daily for comprehension practice.
bullets: Week 1: Quant — simplification, approximation, percentages, ratio; Reasoning — inequalities, coding-decoding, direction; English — reading comprehension basics, grammar rules
Week 2: Quant — number series, quadratic equations, averages; Reasoning — linear and circular seating; English — error spotting, cloze test
Week 3: Quant — profit and loss, simple and compound interest, time and work; Reasoning — floor and box puzzles, syllogism; English — para jumbles, fillers
Week 4: Quant — speed, time and distance, mixtures, data interpretation (tables, bar); Reasoning — blood relations, order and ranking, mixed puzzles; first full-length mock at the weekend
Week 5: Quant — DI (pie, line, caselet), probability, mensuration; Reasoning — scheduling puzzles, data sufficiency; English — RC speed work; two mocks this week
Week 6: Sectional tests in your weakest section every day; revise all formulas; two to three mocks
Week 7: One full mock every alternate day with deep analysis; targeted practice on errors
Week 8: Daily full mock in the exam time slot, light revision, no new topics in the final three days

sections.heading: Mock tests and revision schedule
paragraphs: From week four, taking full-length timed mock tests and reviewing the explanations becomes the centre of your preparation. A mock is only useful if you spend at least as long analysing it as taking it. For each wrong or skipped question, ask: was it a concept gap, a calculation slip, or a poor choice to attempt it at all?
Keep an error notebook with three columns: topic, mistake and fix. Revise it every Sunday. Over eight weeks this notebook becomes your most valuable revision material.
bullets: Weeks 1–3: sectional practice only, 20–25 questions per topic
Week 4: 1 full mock
Week 5–6: 2–3 full mocks per week
Weeks 7–8: 4–6 full mocks per week
Every Sunday: error-notebook revision and formula sheet

sections.heading: Section-wise tips
paragraphs: Quant: memorise squares to 30, cubes to 20 and fraction-percentage equivalents up to 1/20; these alone save minutes in simplification and DI. Reasoning: practise drawing puzzle diagrams quickly and learn to spot which puzzle is solvable in under five minutes. English: read actively, summarise each paragraph in a phrase, and learn common grammar rules rather than lists of rare words.
Speed comes from repetition. Time yourself on every practice set, even early on, so that working under the clock feels normal by the time you start mocks.

In Reasoning, practise puzzles in increasing order of difficulty: start with simple linear arrangements, then circular, then floor and box, and finally scheduling puzzles with months or days. In English, keep a short list of grammar rules you get wrong in practice and revise it before every mock. In Quant, learn to recognise DI questions that need only approximate values; calculating exactly when the options are far apart wastes time that you will need later in the section.

sections.heading: If you are a beginner or working full-time
paragraphs: If you are starting from scratch, spend the first two weeks only on basics: arithmetic concepts, simple puzzles and grammar. If you work full-time, two hours on weekdays and six on weekends is enough for a 60-day plan, but you will need to cut sectional practice slightly and protect your mock-test days.
Whatever your situation, consistency matters more than long weekend marathons. A fixed daily slot builds the habit that carries you through eight weeks.

sections.heading: How to analyse a mock test properly
paragraphs: A good analysis follows the same steps every time. First, record attempts, correct answers and accuracy for each section. Second, re-solve every question you skipped without the timer; if you can solve it in under a minute, your selection was the problem, not your knowledge. Third, read the explanation for every wrong answer and write the fix in your error notebook.

Finally, look at time. Note which puzzle or DI set took longest and whether it was worth it. Over several mocks, you will see a pattern — perhaps you over-invest in the first puzzle, or rush English. Fixing that pattern is often worth five to ten marks.

sections.heading: Keep official details in view
paragraphs: Patterns, sectional timings and eligibility can change between cycles. Check ibps.in for the latest notification before you finalise your plan, and download the official information handout once it is released.

faqs: Can I clear IBPS PO prelims in 60 days?

Sixty days is enough to cover the prelims syllabus and build speed if you study three to four hours daily and take regular mocks from week four. No plan can promise a result, but a steady schedule with honest mock analysis gives you a realistic chance, even as a first-time candidate.
Which section is most important in IBPS PO prelims?

All three matter because sectional cut-offs have applied in recent cycles. Quant and Reasoning usually carry more questions, with DI and puzzles being the highest-weight topics. English is often the most scoring for strong readers. Build a minimum comfort level in each before trying to maximise one.
How many mock tests should I take for IBPS PO?

Aim for around 20 to 25 full-length mocks across the last five weeks, plus sectional tests. The number matters less than the analysis: review every mock carefully, note why you lost marks and fix those topics before the next test.

guides.title: IBPS PO vs SBI PO: Differences and Which to Target
guides.description: IBPS PO vs SBI PO compared: exam pattern, difficulty, syllabus overlap and preparation tips, so you can decide which to prioritise and prepare for both.
secondary: difference between ibps po and sbi po
sbi po vs ibps po which is better
ibps po and sbi po syllabus
sbi po vs ibps po difficulty
guides.intro: IBPS PO vs SBI PO is one of the most common questions bank aspirants ask, and the honest answer is that most serious candidates prepare for both. The two exams recruit probationary officers, share almost the same syllabus and test similar skills. They differ in who conducts them, which banks you join, how the papers feel and how the final selection works. This guide compares the two clearly, explains where the preparation overlaps and where it differs, and helps you decide how to prioritise if your time is limited. For eligibility, dates and vacancies, always rely on ibps.in and sbi.co.in/careers.

sections.heading: Who conducts each exam and where you work
paragraphs: IBPS PO is conducted by the Institute of Banking Personnel Selection for participating public sector banks. After the final result, candidates are allotted to one of these banks based on merit and preference. SBI PO is conducted by the State Bank of India for its own recruitment, so selected candidates join SBI directly.

That single difference shapes a lot: the work culture, postings and career path are those of the bank you join. If you have a strong preference for SBI, its exam is your direct route; if you are open to several public sector banks, IBPS PO widens your options. Many candidates simply write both.

Both roles are officer-grade positions with responsibility for branch operations, customers and, over time, credit and team management. Postings and transfers follow each bank's policies, which you can read about on the respective career pages. Think about where you are willing to work and the kind of organisation you prefer, not only about which exam seems easier.

sections.heading: Exam pattern compared (indicative)
paragraphs: Both prelims are structured similarly in our mock tests: 100 questions, 100 marks, 60 minutes and 0.25 negative marking, across English, Quantitative Aptitude and Reasoning. Both have used sectional time limits in recent cycles. This is indicative — confirm in the latest official notification for each exam.

The mains and the final stage differ more. Both mains papers include objective sections and a descriptive component, and both have a later interview stage, while SBI has also included a group exercise in some cycles. Check the current notification, because these stages are revised from time to time.
bullets: Prelims sections: English, Quant, Reasoning in both (indicative)
Prelims questions and time: 100 in 60 minutes in both (indicative)
Negative marking: 0.25 per wrong answer in both (indicative)
Final stage: interview for IBPS PO; SBI has used group exercise plus interview in some cycles

sections.heading: Difficulty and paper style
paragraphs: Candidates generally find SBI PO slightly tougher, especially in Reasoning and Quant, where puzzles and data interpretation sets tend to be longer and more calculation-heavy. IBPS PO prelims is often described as more balanced, though the difficulty varies by year and shift.

In English, SBI PO has often leaned towards longer reading comprehension passages and inference-based questions, while IBPS PO tests a mix of RC, cloze and grammar. These are tendencies, not rules; prepare for both styles.

Remember that difficulty is relative to everyone else in your shift. A harder paper usually means fewer attempts across the board, so the aim on the day is to make good choices and keep accuracy high, not to match the attempts you managed in an easier mock.

sections.heading: Syllabus overlap: one preparation, two exams
paragraphs: The core syllabus overlaps almost entirely, which is why preparing for one prepares you for the other. Your daily practice in arithmetic, DI, puzzles, inequalities and reading comprehension serves both exams equally.
The main differences appear in emphasis rather than content. SBI papers reward speed on harder puzzles and DI; IBPS papers reward accuracy across a wider spread of moderate questions.
bullets: Common Quant: simplification, number series, quadratic equations, arithmetic, DI
Common Reasoning: puzzles, seating arrangement, inequalities, syllogism, coding-decoding, blood relations
Common English: reading comprehension, cloze test, error spotting, para jumbles, fillers
Extra focus for SBI: harder puzzles, longer DI sets, inference-based RC

sections.heading: Which one should you prioritise?
paragraphs: If you are a beginner, build your base using a moderate-level plan suited to IBPS PO, then raise the difficulty with SBI-level puzzles and DI in the last few weeks. If you are already scoring well in moderate mocks, practise at SBI level from the start, since harder practice makes the IBPS paper feel more comfortable.

Look at the calendar too. Whichever exam comes first in a given year deserves the final-month focus, but do not drop the other. A week of switching to the other exam's style before its date is usually enough.
bullets: Prefer SBI specifically: prioritise SBI PO, write IBPS PO as a parallel chance
Open to any public sector bank: write both; IBPS PO offers more bank options
Beginner: start with IBPS-level difficulty, then move up
Already scoring well: practise at SBI-level difficulty throughout

sections.heading: Preparing for both without burning out
paragraphs: Use a single daily routine for both exams, and switch only your mock tests. Take full-length timed mock tests in the style of the upcoming exam, and review the explanations for every error. Keep one error notebook and one formula sheet rather than separate ones.

In the final fortnight before each prelims, take mocks at the same time of day as your exam slot and practise the sectional order you plan to use. Then reset for the next exam with a day of light revision.

sections.heading: Mains and later stages: what changes
paragraphs: Prelims is a qualifying round in both exams, so your final position depends on mains and the final stage. Both mains papers test reasoning, quantitative aptitude or data analysis, English and general, economy or banking awareness, and include a descriptive paper on letter and essay writing. The weight of each part and the time limits differ, so read each notification carefully.

Because general and banking awareness and descriptive writing are needed in both mains exams, start them early. Fifteen to twenty minutes of news and banking awareness daily, and one essay or letter each week, will serve both exams without disturbing your prelims plan.
bullets: Shared mains areas: reasoning, data analysis, English, general and banking awareness
Descriptive writing: letter and essay in both (confirm in notification)
SBI final stage has included a group exercise in some cycles; IBPS uses an interview

sections.heading: Where to check official details
paragraphs: Eligibility, age limits, the number of attempts, dates and the selection process change between cycles. Read the full notification on ibps.in for IBPS PO and sbi.co.in/careers for SBI PO before applying, and keep both pages bookmarked for updates.

faqs: Is SBI PO tougher than IBPS PO?

Many candidates find SBI PO slightly tougher, with longer puzzles and more calculation-heavy DI, but the difference varies by year. Preparing at SBI-level difficulty once your basics are strong usually makes the IBPS PO paper feel manageable.
Is the syllabus of IBPS PO and SBI PO the same?

The prelims syllabus overlaps almost completely: English, Quantitative Aptitude and Reasoning with the same core topics. Differences appear in emphasis, difficulty and the later stages. Always confirm the current syllabus and stages in each exam's official notification.
Can I prepare for IBPS PO and SBI PO together?

Yes, and most aspirants do. Follow one study routine covering the shared syllabus, and change only the style of your mock tests depending on which exam comes next. Keep a single error notebook so your weak areas improve for both exams at once.

guides.title: How to Prepare for IBPS Clerk Prelims in 45 Days
guides.description: A 45-day IBPS Clerk prelims plan with weekly targets for Numerical Ability, Reasoning and English, plus a mock test and revision schedule built for speed.
guides.primary: how to prepare for ibps clerk prelims
guides.intro: If you want to know how to prepare for IBPS Clerk prelims in a focused way, 45 days of steady work is a sensible target for most graduates. The prelims checks three things — Numerical Ability, Reasoning Ability and English Language — and the questions are moderate in level but tightly timed. That means your plan must build both basics and speed. This guide gives you a six-and-a-half-week schedule with clear weekly targets, explains approximately which topics carry the most marks, and shows when to switch from topic practice to full-length mocks. It assumes about three hours a day; stretch it if you are starting from zero.

sections.heading: IBPS Clerk prelims pattern (indicative)
paragraphs: Our mock tests use an indicative pattern of 100 questions, 100 marks and 60 minutes, with 0.25 of a mark deducted for each wrong answer. Recent cycles have used three sections with separate time limits. This is indicative — confirm in the latest official notification on ibps.in, which also covers eligibility, language options and the schedule.

The level of questions in IBPS Clerk is usually a notch below IBPS PO, but the time pressure is similar. Clerk candidates who do well tend to have very fast calculation and a good eye for which puzzle or DI set to attempt first.
bullets: English Language: about 30 questions (approximately)
Numerical Ability: about 35 questions (approximately)
Reasoning Ability: about 35 questions (approximately)
Negative marking: 0.25 per wrong answer (indicative)

sections.heading: Topic weightage: what decides your score
paragraphs: Based on the syllabus and the usual shape of the paper, simplification and approximation is the single biggest scoring area in Numerical Ability, followed by number series, data interpretation and arithmetic word problems such as percentages, profit and loss, averages, ratio, interest, and time and work. In Reasoning, puzzles and seating arrangements take a large share, with inequalities, syllogism, coding-decoding, alphanumeric series, blood relations and direction sense making up the rest.

In English, reading comprehension and cloze test carry the most questions, alongside error spotting, fillers, word swap and sentence rearrangement. Because the questions are moderate, accuracy in these high-weight areas matters more than attempting rare question types.

sections.heading: The 45-day IBPS Clerk plan, week by week
paragraphs: Divide each day roughly as follows: 70 minutes Numerical Ability, 70 minutes Reasoning, 30 minutes English and 10 minutes of formula or vocabulary revision. Do 20 simplification questions every single day from Day 1; it is the fastest way to build calculation speed.
bullets: Week 1 (Days 1–7): tables, squares, cubes, fractions; simplification, approximation, percentages; inequalities, coding-decoding; basic grammar and RC
Week 2 (Days 8–14): number series, ratio, averages, ages; linear seating, direction, blood relations; error spotting and fillers
Week 3 (Days 15–21): profit and loss, interest, time and work, speed and distance; circular seating, floor and box puzzles; cloze test, para jumbles; first full mock on Day 21
Week 4 (Days 22–28): data interpretation (table, bar, pie), mixtures, quadratic equations; syllogism, order and ranking, alphanumeric series; two mocks
Week 5 (Days 29–35): sectional tests daily in your weakest section; mixed puzzles; RC speed work; three mocks
Week 6 (Days 36–42): one full mock daily with analysis, error-notebook revision
Days 43–45: two light mocks at your exam slot time, formula revision, rest the evening before

sections.heading: How to build speed for the clerk exam
paragraphs: Speed in IBPS Clerk mostly comes from Numerical Ability. Memorise squares up to 30, cubes up to 20, and percentage equivalents of common fractions. Practise approximation by rounding sensibly rather than calculating exact values. In number series, learn to test differences, ratios and alternating patterns in that order.

In Reasoning, draw puzzle diagrams with a consistent shorthand and practise identifying easy puzzles within the first 30 seconds. In English, avoid getting stuck on one hard question; mark it and move on, then return if time remains.
bullets: Daily: 20 simplification + 10 number series questions
Every second day: two puzzles under a five-minute timer each
Daily: one RC passage with a strict time limit
Weekly: one sectional test per section

sections.heading: Mock tests and analysis
paragraphs: From Day 21, taking full-length timed mock tests and reviewing every explanation becomes the core of your plan. After each mock, sort your mistakes into concept gaps, calculation slips and poor question choices. Concept gaps need study; slips need slower checking on easy questions; poor choices need a better attempt order.

Also note your section-wise time use. If you are spending too long on one puzzle or DI set, practise abandoning sets that do not open up quickly. That single habit often adds more marks than learning a new topic.

Keep an error notebook with three columns — topic, what went wrong, and the fix — and revise it every Sunday and again in the final week. By the end of the plan this notebook becomes your most personal and useful revision material, because it lists exactly the mistakes you are most likely to repeat under pressure.

sections.heading: Attempt strategy and negative marking
paragraphs: With 0.25 negative marking in the indicative pattern, random guessing is costly, but a well-reasoned guess after eliminating two options is usually worth taking. Track your accuracy in mocks; if it falls well below the mid-80s percentage range, slow down slightly and attempt fewer but surer questions.
Start each section with the question types you are fastest at — typically inequalities and simplification — to build momentum, then move to puzzles or DI.

sections.heading: Common mistakes clerk aspirants make
paragraphs: The most common mistake is collecting too many books and courses and finishing none. Pick one source per section and complete it. The second is avoiding mocks until you feel fully ready; that moment never comes, and late mocks leave no time to fix weaknesses.

Another frequent error is ignoring the smaller quick-scoring topics such as inequalities, coding-decoding and fillers. They take little time to learn and are among the fastest marks in the paper. Finally, do not neglect sleep in the final week; tired candidates make calculation slips that cost far more than an extra hour of study gains.

sections.heading: Final week checklist
paragraphs: In the last week, stop learning new topics. Revise formulas, your error notebook and your puzzle shorthand. Keep your sleep cycle aligned with your exam slot, and check the admit card, reporting time and ID requirements on ibps.in well in advance.
On the day, read each instruction screen carefully, and if sectional timing applies, use every minute of each section rather than finishing early and waiting.

faqs: Is 45 days enough for IBPS Clerk prelims?

For most graduates with basic school maths and English, 45 days of three focused hours a day is enough to cover the prelims syllabus and complete 20 or more full mocks. If you are starting from zero or can study only an hour daily, give yourself 60 to 75 days instead.
Which section is easiest to score in IBPS Clerk prelims?

It depends on your background. Many candidates score fastest in Numerical Ability once simplification and number series are strong, while good readers find English quickest. Reasoning puzzles take the longest to master. Identify your strongest section through early mocks and protect it while improving the others.
Should I study for IBPS Clerk mains during prelims preparation?

Focus on prelims until the exam, since clearing it comes first. However, reading the news daily and revising banking awareness for 15 to 20 minutes a day helps for mains without affecting your prelims plan. Start dedicated mains preparation immediately after prelims.

guides.intro: IBPS Clerk vs SBI Clerk is a choice many bank aspirants think they have to make, but in practice most write both. The two exams recruit clerical staff, test the same three areas at prelims and share most of their syllabus. They differ in the conducting body, which bank you join, how the papers tend to feel, and parts of the selection process such as the local language test. This guide sets out the differences clearly, shows how one preparation plan can cover both, and helps you prioritise if the dates clash. For eligibility, dates and vacancies, rely only on ibps.in and sbi.co.in/careers.

sections.heading: Who conducts each exam and which bank you join
paragraphs: IBPS Clerk is conducted by the Institute of Banking Personnel Selection for participating public sector banks; after the result, candidates are allotted to a bank, usually within the state they applied for. SBI Clerk, officially the Junior Associate (Customer Support and Sales) recruitment, is conducted by the State Bank of India for its own branches.
Both are state-wise recruitments, so you apply for one state and are generally expected to know its official local language. That makes the choice of state as important as the choice of exam.

sections.heading: Exam pattern compared (indicative)
paragraphs: In our mock tests, both prelims follow the same indicative pattern: 100 questions, 100 marks, 60 minutes and 0.25 negative marking, across English Language, Numerical Ability and Reasoning Ability, with sectional time limits used in recent cycles. This is indicative — confirm in the latest official notification for each exam.

Both mains exams add General or Financial Awareness and a computer or general English component alongside reasoning and quantitative sections. Neither clerk exam has had an interview in recent cycles; instead there is a local language proficiency test for candidates who need it. Confirm every stage in the current notification.
bullets: Prelims sections: English, Numerical Ability, Reasoning in both (indicative)
Prelims: 100 questions in 60 minutes in both (indicative)
Negative marking: 0.25 per wrong answer in both (indicative)
No interview in recent cycles; local language test applies as per notification

sections.heading: Difficulty and paper style
paragraphs: SBI Clerk is often described as slightly tougher at prelims, especially in Reasoning puzzles and in Numerical Ability, where arithmetic word problems can be longer. IBPS Clerk tends to reward speed on a large number of moderate questions, particularly simplification and number series.

In English, both use reading comprehension, cloze tests and error-based questions. SBI Clerk passages have sometimes been longer. Year-to-year variation is large, so do not read too much into one shift; prepare for a moderate-to-moderately-difficult level in both.

Remember that difficulty is relative to the others in your shift. On a tougher paper, attempts fall for everyone, so keep accuracy high and avoid forcing extra attempts just to match your best mock. Practising one harder mock a week helps you stay calm when the actual paper surprises you.

sections.heading: Syllabus overlap and differences in emphasis
paragraphs: At prelims, the overlap is almost complete. Daily practice in simplification, number series, arithmetic, DI, puzzles, inequalities, syllogism and reading comprehension serves both exams equally. Even in mains, the general and financial awareness preparation is shared.
The differences are mostly in emphasis. Expect slightly harder puzzles and arithmetic in SBI Clerk, and a stronger premium on raw calculation speed in IBPS Clerk.
bullets: Shared Numerical Ability: simplification, approximation, number series, arithmetic, DI
Shared Reasoning: puzzles, seating, inequalities, syllogism, coding-decoding, alphanumeric series
Shared English: RC, cloze test, error spotting, fillers, para jumbles
Extra for SBI: harder puzzles and longer arithmetic word problems
Extra for IBPS: maximum simplification and series speed

sections.heading: Which should you prioritise?
paragraphs: If you have a clear preference for SBI's branch network and brand, make SBI Clerk your main target and write IBPS Clerk as a parallel chance. If you are open to any public sector bank in your state, write both and let the calendar decide your final-month focus.

For beginners, start with IBPS-level speed drills to build a base, then add SBI-level puzzles and arithmetic. For candidates already scoring well in moderate mocks, practise at SBI level so that IBPS feels comfortable on the day.

Also consider timing. If the two prelims fall close together, prepare with SBI-level difficulty throughout so that you are ready for either, and switch only your mock style in the final week before each exam.
bullets: Clear SBI preference: SBI Clerk first, IBPS Clerk as backup
Open to any PSU bank in your state: write both with equal effort
Beginner: build speed with IBPS-style drills, then raise difficulty
Experienced: practise at SBI difficulty throughout

sections.heading: One plan for both exams
paragraphs: Use a single daily routine: simplification and series every day, puzzles every day, and one timed RC passage. Change only the style of your mock tests depending on which exam is next. Taking full-length timed mock tests and reviewing the explanations for every mistake will do more for both exams than switching study material.

Keep one error notebook and one formula sheet. In the fortnight before each prelims, take mocks at your exam slot time and practise the section order you intend to use. After the first exam, take a day of light revision and then switch to the second exam's mock style.

sections.heading: Local language and state choice
paragraphs: Both exams expect candidates to know the official language of the state they apply for, and a language test may be conducted for those who did not study it at school. Check the exact rule and the list of languages for each state in the notification before applying.
Choose the state where you can genuinely work and communicate. A state with more posts may look attractive, but language proficiency and comfort with local customers matter for the job.

sections.heading: Mains differences worth knowing
paragraphs: In mains, both exams add general or financial awareness, and both test reasoning, quantitative aptitude and English at a higher level, with computer aptitude combined into one section in recent cycles. The number of questions, sectional timings and marks differ between the two, and they can change each year.

For preparation, the practical difference is small. Daily current affairs, banking awareness and basic computer knowledge serve both exams. If both mains fall close together, revise general awareness continuously and adjust only your mock style for each exam.

sections.heading: Where to check official details
paragraphs: Eligibility, age limits, state-wise posts, dates and the selection process change from cycle to cycle. Read the full notification on ibps.in for IBPS Clerk and sbi.co.in/careers for SBI Clerk before you apply, and check both regularly for updates and corrigenda.

faqs: Is SBI Clerk tougher than IBPS Clerk?

Many aspirants find SBI Clerk prelims slightly tougher, mainly in puzzles and arithmetic, but difficulty changes every year and across shifts. Preparing at SBI-level difficulty after your basics are strong usually covers IBPS Clerk comfortably as well.
Is there an interview in IBPS Clerk or SBI Clerk?

Neither exam has used an interview in recent cycles. Selection has been based on mains performance, subject to a local language proficiency test where applicable. Always confirm the current selection process in the latest official notification, since it can change.
Can I apply for both IBPS Clerk and SBI Clerk?

Yes, eligible candidates can apply for both, since they are separate recruitments. The syllabus overlaps heavily, so one preparation plan serves both. Plan your final weeks around whichever exam comes first, and check each notification for eligibility and state rules.

guides.title: How to Prepare for SBI PO Prelims in 60 Days
guides.description: A 60-day SBI PO prelims preparation plan: weekly targets for Quant, Reasoning and English, high-level puzzle and DI practice, and a mock test schedule.
guides.primary: how to prepare for sbi po prelims
guides.intro: Knowing how to prepare for SBI PO prelims starts with accepting that it is one of the tougher banking prelims: puzzles are longer, data interpretation is heavier and reading passages demand inference. Sixty days is a realistic window to get ready if you study three to four hours daily. This guide gives you an eight-week plan with weekly targets for English, Quantitative Aptitude and Reasoning, explains approximately where the marks lie, and sets out a mock-test and revision schedule. It also covers how to raise your practice level to SBI difficulty without losing accuracy.

sections.heading: SBI PO prelims pattern (indicative)
paragraphs: Our mock tests follow an indicative pattern of 100 questions, 100 marks and 60 minutes, with 0.25 of a mark deducted for each wrong answer, split into English, Quant and Reasoning with sectional time limits as used in recent cycles. Treat this as indicative — confirm in the latest official notification on sbi.co.in/careers, which also lists eligibility and the later stages.
With sectional timing, you cannot borrow time from a strong section to rescue a weak one. Each section needs its own plan and its own attempt strategy.
bullets: English Language: about 30 questions (approximately)
Quantitative Aptitude: about 35 questions (approximately)
Reasoning Ability: about 35 questions (approximately)
Negative marking: 0.25 per wrong answer (indicative)

sections.heading: Where the marks are: approximate weightage
paragraphs: Based on the syllabus and the usual shape of the paper, Reasoning is dominated by puzzles and seating arrangements — often more than half the section — with inequalities, syllogism, coding-decoding, blood relations and direction filling the rest. In Quant, data interpretation sets, quadratic equations, number series and arithmetic word problems carry most of the marks; SBI has often used caselet and missing-data DI.
English typically leans on reading comprehension with inference questions, plus cloze tests, error spotting, para jumbles and word usage. Strong readers can make English their safest section.

sections.heading: The 60-day SBI PO plan, week by week
paragraphs: Split each study day into about 80 minutes of Reasoning, 80 minutes of Quant, 45 minutes of English and 15 minutes of revision. Read one serious long-form article daily and summarise it in two lines.
bullets: Week 1: Quant — simplification, percentages, ratio, averages; Reasoning — inequalities, coding-decoding, direction; English — grammar rules, RC basics
Week 2: Quant — number series (including wrong-number), quadratic equations; Reasoning — linear and circular seating; English — error spotting, cloze
Week 3: Quant — profit and loss, interest, time and work, speed and distance; Reasoning — floor, box and month-based puzzles; English — para jumbles, word usage
Week 4: Quant — table, bar, line and pie DI; Reasoning — syllogism, blood relations, input-output basics; first full mock
Week 5: Quant — caselet and missing-data DI, probability, mensuration; Reasoning — mixed and uncertain-number puzzles; English — inference RC; two mocks
Week 6: SBI-level puzzle and DI sets daily, sectional tests; three mocks
Week 7: four to five mocks with deep analysis, error-notebook revision
Week 8: daily mock at your exam slot, formula and notebook revision, no new topics in the last three days

sections.heading: Raising your level to SBI difficulty
paragraphs: Many candidates do well in moderate mocks and then struggle with SBI's longer sets. The fix is gradual: from week five, include at least one hard puzzle and one hard DI set in every practice session, even if you cannot finish them in time at first.

Learn to judge a set quickly. Read the puzzle's conditions once; if you cannot fix at least two positions within a minute, it may be a set to leave. In DI, check whether the questions need heavy calculation before committing.
bullets: Practise puzzles with uncertain numbers of people or floors
Practise DI where one value must be derived before others
Time every set: target 5–6 minutes per puzzle, 6–7 per DI set
Note which set types you should skip in the exam

sections.heading: Mock-test and revision schedule
paragraphs: From week four, taking full-length timed mock tests and reviewing every explanation is the backbone of your plan. Analyse each mock for at least an hour: list attempted, correct and wrong per section, then classify each error as concept, calculation or selection. Write fixes into your error notebook.
Vary your mocks between moderate and SBI-level difficulty so you learn to stay calm when a paper feels hard. A tough mock is practice in judgement, not a reason to panic.
bullets: Weeks 1–3: topic-wise practice only
Week 4: 1 mock; weeks 5–6: 2–3 mocks per week
Weeks 7–8: 4–6 mocks per week
Every Sunday: error-notebook and formula-sheet revision

sections.heading: Section-wise tips
paragraphs: Reasoning: build a consistent diagram shorthand and attempt the quick topics — inequalities, syllogism, coding — first. Quant: secure quadratic equations, series and simplification early, then move to DI and arithmetic. English: read the RC questions before the passage to know what to look for, and do not over-think vocabulary items.
Across sections, keep accuracy high. Under negative marking, ten careful extra attempts beat twenty careless ones.

In English, keep a short list of grammar rules you repeatedly get wrong and revise it before every mock. In Quant, learn to recognise when approximate values are enough; if the options are far apart, exact calculation wastes time you will need for the next DI set. In Reasoning, practise reconstructing the puzzle quickly from the conditions that fix positions first, such as 'sits at an end' or 'lives on the top floor'.

sections.heading: Common mistakes SBI PO aspirants make
paragraphs: One frequent mistake is preparing only at moderate level and being shocked by the actual paper's longer puzzles. Another is spending too much of the first month on rarely asked topics instead of puzzles, DI and RC, which carry most of the marks. A third is taking mocks without proper analysis, which repeats the same errors.

Also avoid the trap of comparing your scores with others online. Mock difficulty varies widely between providers. Measure progress only against your own earlier scores and accuracy, and keep improving the specific topics your error notebook points to.
bullets: Practise at SBI-level difficulty from week five
Spend the most time on puzzles, DI and RC
Analyse every mock for at least an hour
Compare only with your own past performance

sections.heading: Before the exam
paragraphs: Download your call letter from sbi.co.in/careers, check the reporting time and documents, and keep your sleep aligned with your slot during the final week. Avoid starting new books or topics in the last few days; revision and calm mocks serve you better.

faqs: Is 60 days enough to prepare for SBI PO prelims?

Sixty days is enough for most graduates to cover the syllabus and build speed with three to four hours of daily study and around 20 to 25 full mocks. Beginners who find puzzles and DI difficult may need an additional month to reach SBI-level comfort.
What is the hardest section in SBI PO prelims?

Most candidates find Reasoning the hardest because of long, multi-variable puzzles, followed by DI-heavy Quant. English can be the most scoring for strong readers. Practise hard puzzles daily from the second month to build confidence.
How should I practise for SBI PO puzzles?

Learn a clear diagram shorthand, solve two or three puzzles daily under a timer, and gradually move to uncertain-number and multi-variable puzzles. After each set, review how you could have reached the first fixed position faster; that step is where most time is saved.

guides.title: SBI PO Prelims Exam Strategy and Time Management
guides.description: SBI PO prelims exam strategy: section-wise time management, attempt order, how to handle negative marking and what to do when a section feels tough.
secondary: how to attempt sbi po prelims
guides.intro: A sound SBI PO prelims exam strategy can be worth as many marks as an extra month of study. The paper is short, the sections are separately timed in recent cycles, and difficulty can swing sharply between shifts. Candidates who know exactly how they will split their minutes, which questions they will attempt first and when they will abandon a set tend to outperform those who simply start at question one. This guide explains a practical section-wise time plan, an attempt order for each section, how to handle negative marking, and what to do in the first and last five minutes.

sections.heading: Know the pattern you are planning for
paragraphs: Our mock tests use an indicative pattern of 100 questions, 100 marks and 60 minutes with 0.25 negative marking, across English, Quantitative Aptitude and Reasoning, each with its own time limit as used in recent cycles. This is indicative — confirm in the latest official notification on sbi.co.in/careers, because the number of questions and sectional timings can change.
Sectional timing means you cannot save time in English to spend on Reasoning. Each section is a separate sprint, and your strategy must work within each window.

sections.heading: A minute-by-minute plan for each section
paragraphs: Within each sectional window, use a simple three-pass approach. Pass one picks off quick, sure questions. Pass two tackles the one or two sets you judge most solvable. Pass three uses the remaining time on marked questions where you can eliminate options. Practise this structure in every mock until it becomes automatic.
bullets: English (about 20 minutes, indicative): 4–5 min grammar and fillers, 8–9 min RC, 5–6 min cloze and para jumbles, 1 min review
Quant (about 20 minutes, indicative): 3–4 min quadratic equations and series, 8–10 min one or two DI sets, 5–6 min arithmetic, 1 min review
Reasoning (about 20 minutes, indicative): 3–4 min inequalities, syllogism and coding, 12–14 min two or three puzzles, 2 min review

sections.heading: Attempt order inside each section
paragraphs: Start every section with the question types you solve fastest and most accurately. This builds momentum and banks marks before you face the harder sets. In Quant, that usually means quadratic equations or approximation; in Reasoning, inequalities and syllogism; in English, fillers or error spotting.

Then move to the sets. Read a puzzle or DI set once and decide within about 45 seconds whether to commit. Signs of a good set: clear conditions, few variables and questions that do not need full arrangements. Signs to skip: many uncertain conditions or calculations with awkward numbers.
bullets: Quant: equations and series → simpler DI set → arithmetic → second DI set if time permits
Reasoning: inequalities, syllogism, coding → easiest puzzle → next puzzle
English: fillers, error spotting → RC → cloze and para jumbles

sections.heading: Handling negative marking
paragraphs: With 0.25 negative marking in the indicative pattern, a blind guess among five options roughly breaks even at best and only adds risk, but a guess after eliminating two options usually works in your favour. Make it a rule: attempt only when you have narrowed it down to two choices or are confident.

Track your accuracy in mocks. If it stays above the mid-80s percentage range, you can afford slightly more attempts. If it falls below that, cut attempts and focus on solving fewer questions correctly.

sections.heading: When a section feels tough
paragraphs: SBI papers sometimes include a section that is much harder than mocks. Remember that difficulty applies to everyone in that shift, so a lower attempt count may still be competitive. Panicking and guessing randomly is the most common way candidates lose marks on a hard day.

If the first puzzle you read looks impossible, move on immediately and look for an easier one. Often the second or third set in a section is more approachable. Do not carry stress from one section into the next; each sectional timer is a fresh start.

A practical habit is to keep a mental count of how many questions you are confident about in each section. If that count is lower than usual, do not chase attempts with guesses; instead, look again for the easiest remaining items, such as single questions in a puzzle that can be answered from partial information.

sections.heading: Practising strategy in mock tests
paragraphs: Strategy is a skill you practise, not something you invent on the day. Taking full-length timed mock tests in the same sectional format, and then reviewing the explanations along with your time log, shows you where minutes leak. Record time spent per set in at least five mocks.
Experiment early with attempt orders, then fix one by the last two weeks and stop changing it. A familiar routine reduces decision fatigue in the exam hall.

Treat at least one mock each week as a strategy session rather than a score check. Try a different attempt order or a stricter time cap per set, and compare the result with your usual approach. This is how you discover what works for you before it matters.
bullets: Log time per set and per section after each mock
Mark which sets you should have skipped
Practise a hard mock at least once a week to train composure
Fix your final attempt order two weeks before the exam

sections.heading: The first and last five minutes
paragraphs: The first few minutes of each section set its tone. Do not start with the first question by default; scroll quickly through the section, note where the quick question types are and where the sets are, and begin with the fastest ones. This short scan usually pays for itself within the first few questions.

The last minutes matter too. Do not try to start a fresh puzzle with two minutes left. Instead, return to questions you marked for review where you had already narrowed the options. If sectional timing applies, the system will move you on automatically, so keep an eye on the clock rather than being cut off mid-question.
bullets: First minute: quick scan of the section
Start with your fastest question types
Last two minutes: only marked questions you had narrowed down
Watch the section timer, not just the overall time

sections.heading: Exam-day checklist
paragraphs: Reach the centre well before the reporting time with the call letter and the ID documents specified in the official instructions. Use the instruction-reading time to settle and plan your first section.
Eat lightly, carry water if allowed, and avoid discussing the paper with others between shifts or while waiting. Confirm all rules on your call letter from sbi.co.in/careers.

faqs: How should I manage time in SBI PO prelims?

Treat each section as a separate sprint within its time limit. Spend the first few minutes on quick question types, then commit to one or two puzzle or DI sets you judge solvable, and use the final minute or two on marked questions you can narrow to two options.
How many questions should I attempt in SBI PO prelims?

There is no fixed safe number, because it depends on the difficulty of your shift. Focus on accuracy instead: aim for high accuracy on every attempt and use your mock-test data to know how many questions you can solve reliably in each sectional window.
Should I guess in SBI PO prelims?

With 0.25 negative marking in the indicative pattern, blind guesses usually cost marks. A guess becomes reasonable when you can eliminate at least two options. Practise this rule in mocks and track whether your guesses are helping or hurting your score.

paragraphs: Each day includes about 90 minutes of Numerical Ability, 90 minutes of Reasoning, 45 minutes of English and 15 minutes of revision. Do 20 simplification questions daily throughout; it is the quickest way to improve calculation speed.

paragraphs: From the middle of the month, taking full-length timed mock tests and reviewing the explanations becomes the most valuable part of your day.
