Days 16–20: two mocks; Days 21–28: one mock daily
Days 29–30: one light mock, revision only

sections.heading: Speed and accuracy tips
paragraphs: In Numerical Ability, round sensibly in approximation questions and learn to spot series patterns by testing differences and ratios first. In Reasoning, attempt inequalities and syllogism early and choose puzzles that open up within a minute. In English, read RC questions before the passage and avoid lingering on any one item.
With negative marking, attempt only when you can eliminate at least two options. Track your accuracy in mocks and adjust your attempt count accordingly.

For calculation speed, learn squares up to 30, cubes up to 20 and percentage values of common fractions such as one-eighth or one-twelfth. These come up constantly in simplification and DI and save seconds on almost every question.

sections.heading: What to skip in a 30-day plan
paragraphs: A month is short, so you must be deliberate about what you leave out. Rarely asked or very time-consuming topics — complex probability, advanced mensuration, unusual puzzle types — can wait until after prelims or be skipped. Do not spend a day on a topic that might bring one question.

Similarly, avoid switching study material midway. One reliable source per section, completed fully, is better than three started and abandoned. If a topic still feels weak after two focused sessions, move on and return to it in revision rather than letting it eat into your schedule.
bullets: Skip or postpone: complex probability, rare puzzle types, advanced mensuration
Keep: simplification, series, DI, arithmetic, puzzles, inequalities, RC, cloze
One source per section, completed fully
Two sessions maximum on any stubborn topic before moving on

sections.heading: Staying consistent for 30 days
paragraphs: A short plan fails most often because of a missed day that turns into three. Set a fixed start time, keep your phone away during study blocks, and track each day's targets on a simple checklist. If you do miss a day, do not try to double the next day's load; carry over only the highest-weight tasks.

sections.heading: Language test and official details
paragraphs: SBI Clerk is a state-wise recruitment, and candidates are expected to know the official local language of the state they apply for; a language test may apply. Read the state-wise rules carefully in the notification on sbi.co.in/careers before applying, and check the site regularly for call letters and updates.

faqs: Can I prepare for SBI Clerk prelims in 30 days?

Yes, if you already have school-level maths and basic English, and can study about four focused hours a day. Prioritise high-weight topics, start full mocks by Day 15, and analyse every mock. Beginners with weaker basics should allow 45 to 60 days instead.
Which topics give the most marks in SBI Clerk prelims?

Based on the syllabus, simplification and approximation, number series and DI lead in Numerical Ability; puzzles and seating arrangement lead in Reasoning; and reading comprehension, cloze test and error spotting lead in English. Secure quick topics first, then build puzzle and DI skills.
How many mock tests should I take for SBI Clerk in 30 days?

Around 12 to 15 full-length mocks from Day 15 to Day 30 is realistic, alongside sectional tests. Taking more without proper analysis gives limited benefit. Spend at least as long reviewing each mock as you did taking it.

guides.title: SBI Clerk Syllabus Explained Section by Section
guides.description: SBI Clerk syllabus explained for prelims and mains: every topic in English, Numerical Ability and Reasoning, with approximate weightage and how to study it.
secondary: sbi clerk exam pattern and syllabus
guides.intro: The SBI Clerk syllabus is short to list but wide in practice. Prelims tests English Language, Numerical Ability and Reasoning Ability, and mains adds General or Financial Awareness and General English along with harder reasoning and quantitative questions. Knowing what each topic actually involves, and approximately how much it counts, helps you study the right things in the right order. This guide explains the prelims syllabus section by section, outlines the mains additions, and suggests how to turn the syllabus into a study plan. Always confirm the latest syllabus in the official notification on sbi.co.in/careers.

sections.heading: Exam structure in brief (indicative)
paragraphs: SBI Clerk is the Junior Associate (Customer Support and Sales) recruitment. Our mock tests use an indicative prelims pattern of 100 questions, 100 marks and 60 minutes, with 0.25 negative marking and sectional time limits as used in recent cycles. Indicative — confirm in the latest official notification.
Mains is a separate, longer paper with its own sections, and a local language proficiency test may apply. Final selection details are set out in each year's notification.

sections.heading: English Language syllabus
paragraphs: English tests reading, grammar and sentence sense rather than rare vocabulary. Reading comprehension usually carries the most questions, with passages on economy, society or general topics. Cloze tests check vocabulary in context and grammar together.

Grammar-based questions include error spotting, sentence improvement and fillers. Arrangement questions include para jumbles and sentence rearrangement. Word-usage items such as word swap or contextual meaning appear in some cycles.

Vocabulary is best built from reading rather than word lists. Read one editorial or long article daily, note four or five unfamiliar words with the sentence in which they appeared, and revise them weekly. This helps both RC and cloze questions.
bullets: Reading comprehension: main idea, detail, inference, tone, vocabulary in context
Cloze test: one passage, several blanks
Error spotting and sentence improvement: subject-verb agreement, tenses, prepositions, articles
Fillers and word usage
Para jumbles and sentence rearrangement

sections.heading: Numerical Ability syllabus
paragraphs: This section rewards calculation speed. Simplification and approximation is usually the biggest block, followed by number series and data interpretation. Arithmetic word problems cover the standard topics from school and early college maths.

Quadratic equations, where you compare two variables, appear in many banking papers and are quick marks once practised. DI typically uses tables, bar graphs, pie charts or line graphs with percentage and ratio calculations.

Simplification questions usually involve fractions, decimals, percentages, squares, cubes and roots, so memorising tables and common values is part of the syllabus in practice. Approximation questions allow rounding, which is a skill worth practising separately.
bullets: Simplification and approximation (approximately the largest share)
Number series: missing and wrong-number series
Data interpretation: table, bar, line, pie, caselet
Arithmetic: percentages, ratio and proportion, averages, ages, profit and loss, simple and compound interest, time and work, speed and distance, mixtures, partnership
Quadratic equations and basic mensuration and probability

sections.heading: Reasoning Ability syllabus
paragraphs: Reasoning is dominated by puzzles and seating arrangements: linear, circular, floor-based, box-based and scheduling puzzles. These take the most time and carry the largest share of marks in the section, approximately.
The remaining questions come from quick topics that you should aim to solve in under a minute each.

Puzzle types vary between cycles, so practise a range: people sitting in rows or around tables, floors of a building, boxes stacked one above another, and schedules across days or months. The method — fixing definite positions first — stays the same.
bullets: Puzzles and seating arrangement (approximately the largest share)
Inequalities: direct and coded
Syllogism, including 'only a few' and possibility cases
Coding-decoding and alphanumeric series
Blood relations, direction sense, order and ranking

sections.heading: What mains adds
paragraphs: Mains repeats reasoning, quantitative aptitude and English at a higher level and adds General or Financial Awareness, which covers current affairs, banking and financial terms, and static general knowledge. Recent cycles have combined reasoning with computer aptitude. Confirm the current mains sections and timings in the official notification.
General awareness cannot be crammed in a week, so read the news and a banking-awareness summary for 15 to 20 minutes daily, even while preparing for prelims.

For computer aptitude, revise basics such as hardware and software terms, operating systems, MS Office features, internet and networking terms, and common keyboard shortcuts. Questions are usually factual and quick, so a compact set of notes revised regularly is enough for most candidates.

sections.heading: Approximate weightage and study order
paragraphs: Since the official notification lists topics but not marks per topic, use the following as a planning guide based on the syllabus and the usual paper. Study high-weight and quick topics first, then the time-consuming ones.
bullets: First: simplification, inequalities, syllogism, error spotting, fillers
Second: number series, coding-decoding, cloze test, arithmetic basics
Third: puzzles and seating, data interpretation, reading comprehension speed
Ongoing: general and financial awareness for mains

sections.heading: How each section tends to be tested
paragraphs: Knowing the syllabus is half the job; knowing how each topic appears is the other half. In English, RC questions often ask for the main idea, a specific detail and the meaning of a word in context, while cloze tests mix vocabulary and grammar. In Numerical Ability, DI questions usually test percentage change, ratios and averages from the given data, so arithmetic speed carries over directly.

In Reasoning, puzzles typically come as sets of five questions based on one arrangement, so solving the arrangement once correctly earns several marks. Inequalities and syllogism appear as quick stand-alone items. Practising each topic in the form it actually appears makes your preparation far more efficient.
bullets: RC: main idea, detail, inference and vocabulary in context
DI: percentage change, ratio and average from tables and charts
Puzzles: one arrangement, several questions
Quick items: inequalities, syllogism, coding, error spotting

sections.heading: Common syllabus mistakes to avoid
paragraphs: Do not study topics from older or unrelated exam syllabi that are no longer asked, and do not skip a topic just because it was absent in one paper. Use the current notification as your boundary, and give extra time to high-weight topics without ignoring the rest entirely.

sections.heading: Turning the syllabus into practice
paragraphs: Convert each bullet above into a checklist. Practise 20 to 30 timed questions per topic, then mixed sectional tests, and finally full-length timed mock tests with a careful review of explanations for every error. Track which topics cost you the most marks and revisit them weekly.
Use the official notification on sbi.co.in/careers as the final authority on the syllabus, sections and timing, because SBI can revise them between cycles.

faqs: What is the syllabus for SBI Clerk prelims?

Prelims covers English Language (reading comprehension, cloze, error spotting, fillers, para jumbles), Numerical Ability (simplification, series, DI, arithmetic, quadratic equations) and Reasoning Ability (puzzles, seating, inequalities, syllogism, coding, blood relations, direction). Confirm the current syllabus in the official notification.
Is general awareness part of SBI Clerk prelims?

General awareness has not been part of SBI Clerk prelims in recent cycles; it is tested in mains along with financial awareness. Still, start reading daily news early, since mains follows soon after prelims. Check the latest notification for the exact sections.
Which topics are most important in the SBI Clerk syllabus?

Based on the syllabus, simplification, number series and DI in Numerical Ability, puzzles and seating in Reasoning, and reading comprehension and cloze in English carry the most marks. Quick topics like inequalities and error spotting are also important because they score fast.

guides.title: How to Prepare for SSC CGL Tier 1 in 90 Days
guides.description: A 90-day SSC CGL Tier 1 study plan covering Reasoning, General Awareness, Quant and English week by week, with a revision cycle and mock test schedule.
guides.primary: how to prepare for ssc cgl tier 1
guides.intro: Three months is a practical window if you want to know how to prepare for SSC CGL Tier 1 properly. The paper covers four subjects — General Intelligence and Reasoning, General Awareness, Quantitative Aptitude and English Comprehension — and each needs a different kind of work: concepts and formulas for Quant, rules and reading for English, pattern practice for Reasoning, and steady memory work for General Awareness. This guide splits 90 days into three phases, gives week-by-week targets, explains approximately where marks come from, and sets out a mock-test and revision cycle. It assumes about four hours of daily study.

sections.heading: SSC CGL Tier 1 pattern (indicative)
paragraphs: Our mock tests follow an indicative pattern of 100 questions for 200 marks in 60 minutes, with negative marking of 0.25 of a question's marks for each wrong answer. The four sections carry roughly equal numbers of questions. This is indicative — confirm in the latest official notification on ssc.gov.in, which also covers eligibility, posts and later tiers.
With about 36 seconds per question on average, Tier 1 is a speed-and-accuracy test. Your preparation must build fast recall of facts and formulas, not just understanding.
bullets: General Intelligence & Reasoning: about 25 questions
General Awareness: about 25 questions
Quantitative Aptitude: about 25 questions
English Comprehension: about 25 questions
Negative marking: 0.25 of marks per wrong answer (indicative)

sections.heading: Approximate weightage within each subject
paragraphs: Based on the syllabus and the usual paper, Quant leans on arithmetic (percentages, ratio, profit and loss, interest, time and work, speed and distance), advanced maths (algebra, geometry, trigonometry, mensuration) and a little DI. Reasoning covers analogy, classification, series, coding-decoding, blood relations, Venn diagrams, mirror and water images, paper folding, embedded figures and syllogism.

English is built on vocabulary (synonyms, antonyms, idioms, one-word substitution, spellings), grammar (error spotting, sentence improvement, active-passive, narration) and comprehension (cloze, RC). General Awareness spans history, polity, geography, economics, general science, static GK and current affairs.

In practice, arithmetic and advanced maths have each contributed a substantial part of Quant, so neither can be skipped. In Reasoning, non-verbal questions such as mirror images and paper folding are quick to learn and should not be ignored. In English, vocabulary and grammar together usually carry more marks than comprehension, which makes daily vocabulary work worthwhile.

sections.heading: The 90-day plan: three phases
paragraphs: Split the 90 days into a foundation phase, a practice phase and a mock phase. Study all four subjects every week so none falls behind; about 75 minutes Quant, 60 minutes Reasoning, 60 minutes English and 45 minutes General Awareness each day.
bullets: Weeks 1–2: Quant — number system, percentages, ratio, averages; Reasoning — analogy, classification, series; English — parts of speech, error spotting rules; GA — Indian polity basics

Weeks 3–4: Quant — profit and loss, interest, time and work, speed and distance; Reasoning — coding-decoding, blood relations, direction; English — vocabulary lists, idioms; GA — modern Indian history

Weeks 5–6: Quant — algebra and geometry; Reasoning — Venn diagrams, syllogism, non-verbal (mirror, water image, paper folding); English — sentence improvement, voice, narration; GA — geography and economy
Weeks 7–8: Quant — trigonometry, mensuration, DI; Reasoning — mixed practice; English — cloze and RC; GA — general science (physics, chemistry, biology); first full mocks begin in week 7
Weeks 9–10: three mocks per week with deep analysis; revise weak chapters; current affairs of the last six to eight months
Weeks 11–12: four to five mocks per week; formula and vocabulary revision; static GK revision
Final days: one mock a day at your exam slot time, light revision, rest before the exam

sections.heading: Making General Awareness stick
paragraphs: General Awareness is where many candidates either gain a big lead or lose ground, because it cannot be solved by speed — you either know the answer or you do not. Short daily sessions work far better than long weekly ones.
Keep compact notes by subject and revise them in a spaced cycle: the next day, after a week, after a month. Use practice questions to test recall rather than re-reading.
bullets: Daily: 15 minutes of current affairs, 30 minutes of static GK or science
Weekly: 50-question GA quiz from the week's topics
Monthly: full revision of your GA notes

sections.heading: Mock tests and revision cycle
paragraphs: From week seven, taking full-length timed mock tests and reviewing every explanation is the centre of your plan. After each mock, note your time per section and the source of each mistake. In SSC CGL, many errors come from rushing easy questions, so watch for silly mistakes as closely as for gaps in knowledge.

Decide your section order through mocks. Many candidates start with General Awareness or English because those questions are fast, then move to Reasoning and finish with Quant. Try two or three orders and settle on one by week ten.
bullets: Weeks 1–6: topic-wise and sectional practice
Weeks 7–8: one to two mocks per week
Weeks 9–10: three mocks per week
Weeks 11–12: four to five mocks per week
Every Sunday: error notebook, formula sheet and vocabulary revision

sections.heading: Tips for beginners and working candidates
paragraphs: If you are starting from scratch in Quant, spend an extra week on arithmetic basics before moving to advanced maths. If you work full-time, two hours on weekdays and six to seven on weekends can still cover this plan, but extend it to about 120 days.
Whatever your schedule, keep a fixed daily slot and protect your mock days. Consistency over 90 days matters more than any single resource.

sections.heading: Common mistakes SSC CGL aspirants make
paragraphs: Many candidates spend months on Quant and leave General Awareness for the last few weeks. Since GA needs repeated revision to stick, this almost always costs marks. Others memorise long vocabulary lists without revision, forgetting most of them within a month.

Another mistake is not practising under the real time limit until late. Tier 1 gives you very little time per question, so time yourself on every practice set from week one. Finally, avoid skipping analysis after mocks; a mock without review mainly measures your current level rather than improving it.
bullets: Start GA from Day 1, in short daily sessions
Revise vocabulary on a spaced schedule
Time every practice set from the first week
Analyse each mock before taking the next

sections.heading: Official updates
paragraphs: SSC can change the Tier 1 pattern, marking scheme and the structure of later tiers. Check ssc.gov.in for the current notification, exam calendar and admit cards, and rely on it over any third-party summary.

faqs: Is 90 days enough for SSC CGL Tier 1?

For most graduates, 90 days of about four hours daily is enough to cover the Tier 1 syllabus, build speed and complete 25 to 30 full mocks. If your Quant or English basics are weak, or you work full-time, plan for four months instead.
Which section should I attempt first in SSC CGL Tier 1?

Many candidates start with General Awareness or English because they are quick, then do Reasoning and finish with Quant. There is no single right order; test two or three orders in mocks and stick with the one that gives you the best accuracy and time balance.
How do I prepare General Awareness for SSC CGL?

Study daily in short sessions: current affairs for 15 minutes and one static subject such as polity, history, geography or science for 30 minutes. Keep compact notes, revise them on a spaced schedule and test yourself with practice questions instead of re-reading.

guides.title: Toughest Topics in SSC CGL Tier 1 and How to Score
guides.description: The toughest topics in SSC CGL Tier 1 across Quant, Reasoning, English and GA, why candidates lose marks there and practical ways to make them scoring.
secondary: how to score high in ssc cgl tier 1
guides.intro: Every aspirant has a list of SSC CGL toughest topics — the chapters that cost marks in every mock no matter how many times they are revised. For most candidates, that list includes geometry and trigonometry in Quant, a few non-verbal and syllogism types in Reasoning, idioms and one-word substitutions in English, and the vast spread of static General Awareness. This guide explains why these topics are hard, which parts of them carry the most marks approximately, and specific methods to make them reliable. The aim is not to master everything but to convert your weakest areas into steady, predictable marks.

sections.heading: A quick note on the pattern
paragraphs: Our mock tests follow an indicative Tier 1 pattern of 100 questions, 200 marks and 60 minutes, with 0.25 of a question's marks deducted for each wrong answer, across Reasoning, General Awareness, Quantitative Aptitude and English. Indicative — confirm in the latest official notification on ssc.gov.in.
Because negative marking applies, a tough topic is costly in two ways: you may skip easy marks out of fear, or you may attempt and get it wrong. The methods below aim to fix both.

sections.heading: Quant: geometry and trigonometry
paragraphs: Geometry is tough because questions mix several theorems in one figure, and trigonometry because identities and standard values must be recalled instantly. Together with algebra and mensuration, these advanced topics carry a meaningful share of the Quant section, approximately.

The fix is to learn a compact set of results thoroughly rather than many results loosely. Most geometry questions use a small group of properties of triangles, circles and quadrilaterals. In trigonometry, standard angle values, basic identities and the habit of substituting convenient angles solve a large share of questions.
bullets: Geometry: centroid, incentre, circumcentre and orthocentre properties; similar triangles; circle chord, tangent and angle theorems
Trigonometry: values at 0°, 30°, 45°, 60°, 90°; identities; maximum and minimum values; heights and distances
Algebra: identities for squares and cubes, x + 1/x type questions — use value substitution
Practice: 15 questions per day from these areas for four weeks

sections.heading: Quant: time-consuming arithmetic
paragraphs: Arithmetic is not conceptually hard, but questions on time and work, pipes and cisterns, speed and distance and compound interest can take two or three minutes if solved the long way. In a 60-minute paper, that is expensive.

Learn efficient methods: the LCM method for work problems, relative speed for trains and boats, and the successive percentage approach for compound interest over two or three years. Then practise these with a timer until each takes under a minute.

Another useful habit is to read the options before calculating. In many arithmetic questions, the options differ enough that a rough estimate identifies the answer, saving the full calculation for questions that really need it.

sections.heading: Reasoning: non-verbal and syllogism
paragraphs: Many candidates who are comfortable with verbal reasoning lose marks in non-verbal questions — mirror and water images, paper folding and cutting, embedded figures, counting figures and cube problems. Others struggle with syllogism when 'some', 'all' and 'no' combine with possibility cases.

Non-verbal questions improve with sheer volume: solve 20 to 30 a day for two weeks, checking each against the explanation. For syllogism, draw Venn diagrams every time, including the minimum-overlap case, until the patterns become automatic.
bullets: Mirror and water images: track one asymmetric feature
Paper folding: unfold step by step, mirroring each cut
Counting figures: use a systematic labelling method
Syllogism: always test the possibility diagram

sections.heading: English: idioms, one-word substitution and vocabulary
paragraphs: Vocabulary-based questions — synonyms, antonyms, idioms and phrases, one-word substitution and spellings — feel tough because there is no method to fall back on. Either you know the word or you guess. Yet together they carry a large share of the English section, approximately.

Build vocabulary in small, repeated doses. Learn 15 to 20 words or idioms a day with a sentence each, and revise them on a spaced schedule. Grammar questions, by contrast, respond to rules; make a list of the 25 to 30 most tested rules and revise them weekly.

For grammar, error-spotting questions tend to test a predictable set of rules: subject-verb agreement, tenses, prepositions, articles, pronouns and degrees of comparison. Practise 20 such questions a day and write the rule next to every mistake you make.

sections.heading: General Awareness: the widest syllabus
paragraphs: General Awareness is the toughest for many because it has no fixed boundary: history, polity, geography, economics, physics, chemistry, biology, static GK and current affairs. It is also the section where a strong candidate can save the most time, since each question takes only seconds.

Prioritise by approximate frequency: polity, history and general science usually contribute most, with geography and economics close behind. Study in short daily sessions, keep one-page notes per subtopic, and test recall with practice questions.
bullets: Polity: fundamental rights, DPSP, Parliament, important articles
History: modern Indian history and freedom movement first
Science: human body, everyday physics and chemistry
Current affairs: the last six to eight months before the exam

sections.heading: Turning tough topics into scoring topics
paragraphs: Choose two tough topics at a time, not all of them. Spend two weeks on each pair with daily timed practice, then test them inside full-length timed mock tests, reviewing the explanations for every mistake. Keep a simple chart of accuracy per topic across mocks; when a topic stays above 80 percent accuracy for three mocks, move on.

Also decide what to leave. If, after honest effort, a particular question type still takes too long, mark it as a skip-first item and return to it only if time remains. Skipping wisely is part of scoring well.

sections.heading: How to find your own toughest topics
paragraphs: The topics above are tough for most candidates, but your list may differ. After every full mock, tag each wrong or skipped question by subject and topic. After five or six mocks, the topics with the most tags are your real weak areas, and they are where your preparation time will pay off most.

Separate topics you do not understand from topics you understand but solve slowly. The first need concept study from a textbook or class notes; the second need timed drills. Mixing the two leads to wasted hours, such as re-reading theory when the real problem is speed.

sections.heading: Keep official details in view
paragraphs: Topic emphasis shifts from year to year, and SSC may revise the pattern. Check ssc.gov.in for the latest notification and syllabus, and use it as the final reference for what to study.

faqs: Which is the toughest section in SSC CGL Tier 1?

It varies by background, but many candidates find Quantitative Aptitude the toughest because of geometry, trigonometry and time-consuming arithmetic, while others struggle most with the breadth of General Awareness. Use your mock-test data to identify your own weakest section rather than relying on general opinion.
How can I improve in geometry for SSC CGL?

Learn a focused set of theorems on triangles, circles and quadrilaterals thoroughly, draw every figure, and solve 15 timed questions a day for about four weeks. Review each mistake against the explanation and note which property you missed; that list becomes your revision sheet.
Should I skip tough questions in SSC CGL Tier 1?

Skip them in the first pass, not permanently. With negative marking, attempt a tough question only if you can solve it or eliminate at least two options. Return to skipped items after finishing the easier ones, and use mocks to learn which question types you should leave.

guides.title: How to Prepare for CAT in 6 Months: Month-by-Month Plan
guides.description: A 6-month CAT preparation plan with month-by-month targets for VARC, DILR and Quant, a mock test schedule and a revision strategy for working professionals.
guides.primary: how to prepare for cat in 6 months
guides.intro: If you are wondering how to prepare for CAT in 6 months, the good news is that six months is a realistic and common timeline, even alongside a job or final-year studies. CAT tests three areas — Verbal Ability and Reading Comprehension, Data Interpretation and Logical Reasoning, and Quantitative Ability — and rewards judgement as much as knowledge. This guide breaks the six months into clear monthly goals, explains approximately how questions are spread across topics, and sets out when to start mocks and how to analyse them. It assumes about three hours on weekdays and longer sessions on weekends.

sections.heading: CAT pattern (indicative)
paragraphs: Our mock tests follow an indicative pattern of 66 questions, 198 marks and 120 minutes, with three marks for a correct answer and one mark deducted for a wrong multiple-choice answer. Recent CATs have had three sections with separate time limits, and type-in-the-answer (TITA) questions have traditionally carried no negative marking. All of this is indicative — confirm in the latest official notification on iimcat.ac.in.
Sectional time limits mean every section matters on its own. Many IIMs also look at sectional performance, so a lopsided profile is risky.
bullets: VARC: about 24 questions (approximately)
DILR: about 20 questions (approximately)
Quantitative Ability: about 22 questions (approximately)
Marking: +3 correct, −1 wrong MCQ; TITA traditionally no negative (indicative)

sections.heading: Approximate topic weightage
paragraphs: Based on the syllabus and recent papers, reading comprehension forms the bulk of VARC, with para summary, para jumbles and odd-sentence questions making up the rest. DILR is organised as sets of four to six questions each, drawn from arrangements, games and tournaments, tables and charts, and mixed logic puzzles.

In Quant, arithmetic (percentages, ratio, profit and loss, time and work, speed and distance, averages, mixtures, interest) has usually been the largest area, followed by algebra (equations, inequalities, functions, logarithms, progressions), then geometry and mensuration, with number system and modern maths (permutations, combinations, probability, sets) contributing the rest.

This spread shifts a little from year to year, so treat it as a guide to where your time should go first rather than a list of topics you can skip. Arithmetic and algebra together deserve the most Quant time, while in DILR the skill of choosing sets matters more than mastering any single type.

sections.heading: The six-month plan, month by month
paragraphs: Work on all three sections every week. A typical weekday: 60 minutes Quant, 45 minutes DILR, 45 minutes VARC and 30 minutes of reading. Weekends: longer practice and, from month three, mocks.
bullets: Month 1: Quant — arithmetic fundamentals and number system; DILR — two sets a day of simple arrangements and tables; VARC — daily reading habit, two RC passages a day
Month 2: Quant — algebra (equations, inequalities, functions); DILR — games, tournaments, Venn and grid puzzles; VARC — para jumbles and summaries, RC on unfamiliar subjects
Month 3: Quant — geometry, mensuration, progressions; DILR — mixed sets under time; VARC — inference and tone questions; first full mock and one sectional per week
Month 4: Quant — modern maths, logarithms, revisit arithmetic; DILR — set selection practice; VARC — speed with accuracy; one mock per week with analysis
Month 5: two mocks per week, topic revision based on mock errors, sectional tests in your weakest area
Month 6: two to three mocks per week, revise formulas and error notebook, last week light practice only

sections.heading: Reading habit for VARC
paragraphs: VARC cannot be crammed. Reading dense, unfamiliar material — essays on philosophy, economics, science, art and society — builds the comprehension and stamina that RC demands. Read 30 to 45 minutes daily from month one.
After each article, write a two-line summary and note the author's main argument and tone. This trains exactly the skills RC and para-summary questions test.

sections.heading: Mock tests and analysis
paragraphs: Mocks are where CAT preparation becomes real. Taking full-length timed mock tests and reviewing every explanation teaches you section-wise time management, set selection in DILR and question selection in Quant. Spend two to three hours analysing each mock: re-attempt questions you skipped, check whether wrong answers were concept or reading errors, and note sets you should have chosen instead.
Track sectional scores and accuracy over time. Improvement is rarely linear; focus on trends across five or six mocks rather than any single score.

Keep a mock log with sectional scores, attempts, accuracy and three takeaways from each test. Before every new mock, read the last three entries. This keeps your analysis from becoming a forgotten notebook and ensures each mock builds on the previous one.
bullets: Months 1–2: topic practice and sectional tests only
Month 3: one full mock every two weeks
Month 4: one mock per week
Month 5: two mocks per week
Month 6: two to three mocks per week, tapering in the last week

sections.heading: For working professionals
paragraphs: If you work full-time, keep weekdays for concept learning and practice in two shorter blocks — early morning and late evening — and use weekends for mocks and analysis. Two to three hours on weekdays and six to eight hours across a weekend is enough for this plan.
Protect your mock days from social and work commitments in months five and six. A missed mock can be rescheduled, but a missed analysis loses most of the value.

sections.heading: Common mistakes in CAT preparation
paragraphs: The most common mistake is collecting too many resources. Pick one main source for concepts in each section and a single mock series, and finish them. Another is postponing mocks until the syllabus feels complete; in CAT, mocks teach selection and time management that concept study cannot.

Many candidates also neglect VARC because it feels unpredictable, or DILR because it seems to depend on luck. Both improve steadily with regular, timed practice. Finally, avoid comparing your mock percentiles with others on forums; focus on your own trend and on fixing the specific mistakes your analysis reveals.
bullets: One concept source per section, one mock series
Start mocks by month three
Practise VARC and DILR daily, not only Quant
Track your own trend, not others' scores

sections.heading: Official details and final weeks
paragraphs: Registration windows, the number of questions, sectional timings and test-centre rules can change from year to year. Check iimcat.ac.in for the latest notification and admit card details. In the final week, avoid new topics, take one or two light mocks, and keep your sleep aligned with your test slot.

faqs: Is 6 months enough to prepare for CAT?

Yes, six months is a common and realistic timeline for most candidates, including working professionals, if you study consistently and take 20 or more mocks with proper analysis. Candidates with weak maths or reading habits may benefit from starting a little earlier.
How many hours a day should I study for CAT?

About three hours on weekdays and six to eight hours across the weekend works for most candidates over six months. The quality of practice and mock analysis matters more than raw hours, so keep sessions focused and track your progress section by section.
When should I start taking CAT mock tests?

Start with an occasional full mock around the third month, once you have covered core concepts, then increase to one a week and finally two or three a week in the last two months. Analyse each mock thoroughly before taking the next one.

guides.title: CAT Exam Day Strategy and Time Management Tips
guides.description: CAT exam day strategy: how to manage time in VARC, DILR and Quant, choose DILR sets, handle TITA questions and stay calm when a section goes badly.
guides.intro: A clear CAT exam day strategy often separates candidates with similar preparation. With three sections on separate timers, sets that vary sharply in difficulty and a marking scheme that punishes careless attempts, how you use your minutes matters as much as what you know. This guide sets out a practical time plan for VARC, DILR and Quant, explains how to choose DILR sets and Quant questions, how to treat TITA questions, and how to recover when a section feels difficult. Practise these ideas in mocks before the exam; strategy that has not been rehearsed rarely holds up under pressure.

sections.heading: Pattern you are planning for (indicative)
paragraphs: Our mock tests follow an indicative pattern of 66 questions, 198 marks and 120 minutes, with three sections on separate timers, three marks per correct answer and one mark deducted for a wrong multiple-choice answer. TITA questions have traditionally carried no negative marking. Indicative — confirm in the latest official notification on iimcat.ac.in.
Separate timers mean you cannot move between sections. Each section is a 40-minute block (indicative) with its own plan.

sections.heading: VARC: a 40-minute plan
paragraphs: Reading comprehension carries most of the VARC marks, so give RC the larger share of time and handle verbal ability questions efficiently. Start with the passage that looks most readable to you; a good first passage builds rhythm.

For each passage, read actively, summarising each paragraph in a few words. Answer questions by returning to the specific lines rather than relying on memory. In para jumbles and odd-sentence questions, look for linking words and pronoun references first.

If you find a passage unusually dense, it is reasonable to leave it for later and return if time allows. Passages on familiar subjects often take far less time, so the order in which you attempt them can change your score noticeably.
bullets: About 26–28 minutes: RC passages (choose order by readability)
About 10–12 minutes: para summary, para jumbles, odd sentence
Last 1–2 minutes: review marked questions
Skip an RC question if two options remain equally strong after a re-read

sections.heading: DILR: set selection is everything
paragraphs: DILR is where strategy matters most. You will rarely solve every set, so the first few minutes of scanning are crucial. Spend about four to five minutes reading the opening lines of all sets and ranking them by apparent ease: clear data, fewer variables and questions that do not need the complete arrangement.

Commit to your top two sets and solve them carefully, then move to a third. If a set does not open up within five or six minutes, step away and try the next one. Two fully solved sets often score better than four half-solved ones.
bullets: Minutes 0–5: scan every set, rank by ease
Minutes 5–30: solve two to three chosen sets carefully
Minutes 30–38: attempt a further set or partial questions from it
Minutes 38–40: check answers in TITA questions

sections.heading: Quant: two passes
paragraphs: Quant rewards selection. In the first pass, move through all questions, solving those that look direct within about two minutes and marking those that need longer. In the second pass, return to the marked questions in order of how promising they looked.
Avoid getting stuck. If a question is still unresolved after three minutes, leave it. Use options wisely in multiple-choice questions — substituting values or checking extremes often saves time.

Distribute your attempts across topics rather than spending all your time on a single area. A mix of arithmetic, algebra and geometry questions in your first pass usually gives a more stable score than relying on one strength.
bullets: Pass 1 (about 25 minutes): quick and sure questions
Pass 2 (about 13 minutes): marked questions, best first
Final 2 minutes: re-check TITA entries for typing errors

sections.heading: Negative marking and TITA questions
paragraphs: With one mark deducted for a wrong MCQ answer against three for a right one (indicative), a guess after eliminating two of four options has a positive expected value, while a blind guess is roughly break-even and adds risk. Attempt MCQs when you have a sound basis, not on hope.

TITA questions have traditionally carried no negative marking, so if you have made real progress on one, enter your best answer rather than leaving it blank. Confirm the current marking scheme on iimcat.ac.in before relying on this.

sections.heading: When a section goes badly
paragraphs: Almost every candidate meets a section that feels harder than expected. Remember that everyone in your slot faces the same paper, and the scoring process accounts for that. The worst response is panic-driven guessing; the best is to slow down, find the easiest remaining questions and secure them.
When the timer ends, let the section go completely. The next section starts at zero, and carrying frustration forward is how one bad section becomes two.

sections.heading: Rehearse your strategy in mocks
paragraphs: Taking full-length timed mock tests and reviewing the explanations is how this strategy becomes instinct. After each mock, note time per RC passage, which DILR sets you chose and whether better ones were available, and how many Quant questions you abandoned too late.
Fix your section plans about three weeks before the exam and stop experimenting. In the final week, take mocks at the same time of day as your slot and treat each as a dress rehearsal.
bullets: Record time per RC passage and per DILR set
After each mock, re-solve the sets you skipped to check your selection
Keep a one-page 'rules for exam day' sheet and refine it
Practise one tough mock a week to build composure

sections.heading: Common time traps in CAT
paragraphs: A few traps catch candidates every year. In VARC, spending too long on one difficult passage leaves no time for an easier one later. In DILR, persisting with a set because you have already invested ten minutes in it is the classic sunk-cost error. In Quant, a single long calculation can quietly consume five minutes.

The common fix is a personal time limit for each unit of work: a passage, a set or a question. When you hit the limit, make a decision — finish quickly, mark and move, or abandon. Practising this rule in mocks makes it automatic on exam day.
bullets: Set a time cap per RC passage, per DILR set and per Quant question
Do not continue a set just because you have invested time in it
Keep an eye on the section timer every few minutes

sections.heading: On the day itself
paragraphs: Check your admit card, reporting time, ID requirements and centre rules on iimcat.ac.in in advance. Reach early, use the waiting time to stay calm rather than revising, and settle your plan for VARC before the timer starts.

faqs: How should I manage time in the CAT exam?

Treat each section as a separate timed block. In VARC, give most of your time to RC; in DILR, spend the first few minutes scanning and ranking sets; in Quant, use two passes, solving quick questions first and returning to marked ones. Rehearse this plan in mocks.
How many DILR sets should I attempt in CAT?

There is no fixed number. Most candidates do better by solving two or three sets accurately than by touching every set. Spend the first few minutes ranking sets by ease, then commit to the best ones and move on if a set does not open up within five or six minutes.
Should I attempt TITA questions in CAT?

TITA questions have traditionally carried no negative marking, so if you have made meaningful progress, enter your best answer. Do not spend excessive time on a TITA question at the cost of easier ones. Confirm the current marking scheme in the official notification before your exam.
